sysd-found-087.title: Latency: why every system has some delay
sysd-found-087.text: No signal travels faster than light, so any system with distance between cause and effect has some delay built in. Latency is the time delay between a cause and its effect in a system, such as the wait between sending a request and seeing the response. Physically, it is a consequence of the limited speed at which any interaction can propagate, and that speed never exceeds the speed of light. The precise definition depends on the system being observed. In communications, the lower limit of latency is set by the medium used to transfer the information. Networks with relatively small delays are called low-latency networks, and the others are high-latency networks. Delay is not only about distance. Mechanical latency is limited by physics too: a disk read waits for the arm's seek time and then for the platter's rotational latency. In multitasking computers, a process can be postponed while other processes run, and the operating system schedules when each action happens, which adds software latency. People notice. Perceptible latency strongly affects user satisfaction and usability, and for high-scale user-facing systems high latency means a big loss of revenue.

sysd-found-099.title: Bandwidth: a ceiling, not the speed you get
sysd-found-099.text: A channel rated at x bit/s may not carry data at rate x. In computing, bandwidth is the maximum rate of data transfer across a given path. Protocols, encryption and other factors add overhead, TCP's three-way handshake adds more for each transaction, and lost packets cut useful throughput further. Useful throughput is therefore less than or equal to the actual channel capacity minus implementation overhead. The word is slippery. It may be called network, data or digital bandwidth, which differs from signal bandwidth, the frequency range in hertz used in signal processing and wireless communications. In web hosting it often means the data transferred to or from a site in a period, such as gigabytes per month. The more accurate phrase is monthly data transfer. The maximum physical-layer speeds of common links are 100 Mbit/s for Fast Ethernet and 1 Gbit/s for Gigabit Ethernet. They are 10 Gbit/s for 10 Gigabit Ethernet and 100 Gbit/s for 100 Gigabit Ethernet.

sysd-found-088.title: Network latency: distance, hops and queues
sysd-found-088.text: Even at the speed of light, distance costs time. Network latency is the delay for data to cross a network, measured one way from source to destination or as the round-trip delay time. Round-trip is quoted more often, because it can be measured from a single point. Light in optical fiber travels at about two thirds of its vacuum speed, which works out to about 5.0 μs of latency per kilometer. In a vacuum light takes 3.33 μs per kilometer. Fiber rarely runs in a straight line, and amplifiers or regenerators added beyond 100 kilometers add their own latency. A packet crosses several links and gateways that each wait for the whole packet. Minimal latency is therefore the sum of each link's transmission delay plus each gateway's forwarding latency. Queuing and processing delays join in, making the profile complex and variable. A geostationary satellite adds about a quarter of a second each way, while a low Earth orbit satellite 400 km up adds about 12 ms.

sysd-found-192.title: Percentile: the value that beats a given share of the data
sysd-found-192.text: Internet providers bill burstable bandwidth at the 95th or 98th percentile, which cuts off the top 5% or 2% of peaks each month. Infrequent peaks are ignored, so the customer is charged more fairly. A percentile is a value greater than a given percentage of all the values in a sample. The 97th percentile, for instance, is above 97% of the data points. The 50th percentile is the median, and the 25th and 75th are the quartiles. A percentile is stated in the unit of the measured values, not in percent. There is no standard definition. Some methods return a score that exists in the data, as nearest rank does, and others interpolate between scores. All give similar results when the sample is very large. Engineers also use percentiles on the numbers a running system reports about itself. The 99th percentile response time over a small window, such as one minute, can give a very early signal of saturation.

sysd-found-089.title: Tail latency: when the average hides the slow requests
sysd-found-089.text: A web service with a 100 ms average latency at 1,000 requests per second may still have 1% of its requests taking 5 seconds. That gap is what tail latency names. Tail latency is the high-percentile response time of a system, usually measured at the 95th, 99th or 99.9th percentile rather than as an average. Average and median latency can mislead in software systems, because a few outliers distort them. In distributed systems, cloud computing and large-scale web services, even a small number of slow requests can make user experience and system performance much worse. The causes are often resource contention, network variability, garbage collection pauses and hardware heterogeneity. Managing it is a major design problem, because lowering average latency does not always improve worst-case performance. Common ways to lessen it are request hedging, adaptive timeouts and the techniques of {{ref:sysd-scale-043}} and {{ref:sysd-blocks-112}}. It matters most for search engines, financial systems and real-time services, where service-level objectives are often based on high-percentile latencies.

sysd-found-097.title: Latency numbers to know, from nanoseconds to 100 ms
sysd-found-097.text: A read from RAM takes about 100 ns, while a packet sent from California to the Netherlands and back takes about 100 ms. Rough figures like these let a designer judge which steps of a system are slow. They are not accurate: they come from online benchmarks, including Jeff Dean's latency numbers, plus other sources. L1 and L2 caches take 1 ns and 10 ns and are usually built onto the microprocessor chip. Unless you work with hardware directly, you probably do not need to worry about them. Sending 1K bytes over a 1 Gbps network takes about 10 μs. Reading from an SSD takes about 100 μs. An insert into a data store takes about 1 ms, since it must store the data, create the index and flush logs. The long trip to the Netherlands and back is like the delay on a long-distance Zoom call. Retry or refresh intervals, by comparison, are on the order of 1-10 s.

sysd-found-094.title: Design trade-offs: every choice costs something
sysd-found-094.text: There is no right or wrong system design. Everything in system design is a trade-off and a compromise, so every design is a compromise between competing goals. Important trade-offs include cost versus performance, reliability versus the ability to scale, performance versus consistency, security versus flexibility, and development speed versus quality. The same pattern repeats in smaller choices. Scaling vertically means adding resources such as CPU and RAM to an existing server, while scaling horizontally means adding more servers to the pool. Consistency promises the most recent data every time, while availability keeps the system up even when parts fail. Synchronous processing performs tasks one after another, while asynchronous tasks can run in the background and new tasks start without waiting. Collecting data and handling it all at once, as in daily billing, differs from handling it in real time, as in fraud detection.

sysd-found-095.title: Reducing latency: the standard techniques
sysd-found-095.text: For high-scale user-facing systems, high latency is a big loss of revenue, so engineers rely on a handful of techniques to reduce it. The top strategies are indexing, a load balancer, a CDN, async processing and data compression. An index speeds up data retrieval on a table, at the cost of additional writes and storage space to maintain it. A load balancer distributes tasks over resources, optimizing response time and avoiding overloading some nodes while others sit idle. A CDN is a geographically distributed network of proxies and data centers, and its edge servers sit closer to the end user than traditional servers. Async processing through a queue of messages lets producers add requests without waiting for them to be processed. Compression with gzip reduces the amount of data transferred for web objects. A cache benefits latency, throughput or both, and prefetching that guesses future reads and requests them ahead of time bypasses the latency altogether if done optimally. One limit applies to all of these: propagation time depends on distance, and more bandwidth does not reduce it, as {{ref:sysd-found-194}} explains.

sysd-found-194.title: Round-trip time: what more bandwidth cannot fix
sysd-found-194.text: More bandwidth cannot make a signal arrive sooner than the distance allows. Round-trip time is the time it takes to send a signal plus the time for its acknowledgement to come back. One-way delay is often approximated as half the RTT. RTT is twice the network latency plus a processing delay at the destination. Propagation time depends on distance, while transmission time is message size divided by bandwidth, so more bandwidth shrinks only the second. Networks with both high bandwidth and high RTT hold large amounts of data in transit and need special protocol design, such as the TCP window scale option.
